name: Rafael Young

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thank you for having me, Rafael. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and what you say stays confidential. Could you describe a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Depends on the season, but say it's October. I'm out at first light with the dogs, Bess and Moss, gathering ewes off the hill for sorting. Six hundred ewes, some suckler cows, and the low fields for hay and oats. My grandfather bought Blackstone Farm in 1951, and now it's me, my brother Martin, his boy Daniel, and one hired shepherd.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the hill on a clear morning, when the dogs are working well and you can see three valleys. There's no office in the world that beats that. What wears me out is forms, prices and people in towns telling me how to farm. My wife Rosa does the books, God bless her, or I'd have gone mad years ago.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I've always said: there's no machine that can gather a hill like a good dog and a man who knows the ground. At the mart, the livestock market, the older lads would nod, and the young ones would roll their eyes. I don't go online, so that's as far as it'd go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means my life carries on as it's been, and I thank God for that. I've got maybe seven years before Daniel takes over properly, and I'd like them to be quiet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as always. Keep the flock, keep the dogs, keep putting a bit by each month, we've about four months of costs in the bank. I wouldn't change a thing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Quietly satisfied, I suppose.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Has anyone tried to sell you AI or robots already?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A man came round last year with a tablet, selling collars that tell you where the cows are. I told him I know where my cows are, they're where the grass is. Daniel thought it was interesting, I'll give him that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: So what keeps you up at night in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Lamb prices, same as always. And the weather. Those I understand.

S0.say: He'd say at the livestock market that no machine can gather a hill like a good dog and a man who knows the ground, and he wouldn't go online about it.
S0.think: Privately it means life carries on as before, and he's thankful for about seven quiet years before his nephew takes over properly.
S0.do: Keeps the flock, the dogs and his monthly savings habit unchanged, with about four months of costs banked. Changes nothing about how he farms.
S0.quote: I told him I know where my cows are, they're where the grass is.
S0.fieldNote: Rafael is rooted, devout and proud of three generations on the same land. He has a ready wit and a firm distrust of salesmen. His nephew's interest in technology is a gentle tension that runs through his answers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good luck to them, but farming's not a factory. Every hill's different and you don't learn it from a computer. I'd say people should stand on their own feet and not wait for the government to sort it out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think the big lowland farms would change and we'd mostly be left alone up the hill. Robots don't like rocks and bog. But prices might drop if the lowland lot get cheaper, and that'd hurt.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep farming as I do, no new machines. I'd tighten the belt a little and save a bit more, maybe an extra hundred a month, in case prices fall. And I'd let Daniel try one or two of his gadgets on the low fields if he paid for them himself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not for the hill, but for the prices.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What part of Blackstone would change first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The low fields, maybe, the hay and oats. A robot tractor on flat ground I can believe. Up on the hill, I'll believe it when I see it gather a flock in fog.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Daniel seems more interested in this. Would you let him lead?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: On the low ground, with his own money, yes. That's how my father let me try things. If it works, fair play to him, but the hill stays with the dogs while I'm alive.

S1.say: He'd say good luck to the machine makers but farming isn't a factory, and people should stand on their own feet rather than wait for the government.
S1.think: Privately he thinks big lowland farms would change while hill farms are left mostly alone, though cheaper lowland production could push his prices down.
S1.do: Keeps farming as he does with no new machines and saves an extra hundred a month in case prices fall. Lets his nephew try gadgets on the low fields if he pays for them himself.
S1.feel: Uneasy, not for the hill itself but for prices.
S1.quote: I'll believe it when I see it gather a flock in fog.
S1.fieldNote: His resistance is grounded in real knowledge of hill terrain, not just habit. He makes room for his nephew in a way that mirrors how his own father treated him. Self-reliance is his public creed, and he doesn't look to government.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is man playing God, and I'd say it in church and at the mart. I'd say the big companies have done it for money and they'll answer for it. I still wouldn't ask the government for a handout, I'd want them to stop the companies instead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think it'd be the end of farming as my family knows it. If robots can work the hill in two years, the price of lamb falls to nothing and land gets bought by whoever owns the machines. Four months of savings won't hold off a whole world changing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cut everything at home straight away, no new truck, no help with our daughter Ana's wedding beyond what we'd promised. I'd sit down with Martin and Daniel and decide what we could hold on to. And I'd lean on the church and the family, the way people round here always have.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. It'd be like watching a flood coming up the valley.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Two years is very fast. What would happen to Blackstone?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I don't know. I'd hope the hill gives us a year or two longer than the flat farms. But I'd be lying if I said I could see how we'd keep going once lamb's half the price.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where would you turn for help?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Family first, then the church. Rosa's brother has a bit put by, and the church has helped farm families before, after the floods in 2015. I'd sooner take help from people who know me than from an office in the city.

S2.say: He'd say in church and at the market that this is man playing God, done by big companies for money, and he'd want the government to stop them rather than hand out help.
S2.think: Privately he thinks it would end farming as his family knows it, with lamb prices collapsing and land going to whoever owns the machines, while four months of savings won't hold that off.
S2.do: Cuts household spending straight away, including no new truck and no extra spending on his daughter's wedding. Sits down with his brother and nephew to decide what to hold on to, and leans on family and church for support.
S2.feel: Alarmed, like watching a flood come up the valley.
S2.quote: I'd sooner take help from people who know me than from an office in the city.
S2.fieldNote: His faith shapes his public reaction strongly, and he blames the companies rather than the technology alone. He admits he can't see a way through, which is a real break from his usual confidence. His support system is family and church, never the state.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the same as the fast one, but with more time to pray on it. I'd tell the young farmers to learn a trade on the side, something with their hands that a robot can't do yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years gets me to sixty-three and gives Daniel time to find his feet. It's still a threat to the way we live, but we'd have time to make choices instead of having them made for us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd save hard, about a fifth of what we make, and pay off the loan on the hay shed. I'd make Daniel a full partner within two years so he has a stake in the decisions. And I'd still farm the hill my way, with the dogs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but with my hand on the wheel.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ever think about selling some land while it still has value?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Never. My grandfather didn't buy it to sell it. If anything I'd make sure it passes to Daniel properly, so no company gets it when I'm gone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you put anything in writing about the farm's future?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes. I'd make sure it's tied up in the family, in writing, so it can't be sold off easily.

S3.say: He'd say it's the same as the fast scenario but with more time to pray on it, urging young farmers to learn a hands-on trade on the side.
S3.think: Privately five years gets him to sixty-three and gives his nephew time to find his feet, so the family could make choices instead of having them forced.
S3.do: Saves about a fifth of income and pays off the hay shed loan. Makes his nephew a full partner within two years and puts the land in family hands in writing, while still farming the hill with his dogs.
S3.feel: Anxious, but feeling he has his hand on the wheel.
S3.quote: My grandfather didn't buy it to sell it.
S3.fieldNote: Extra time makes him think about succession rather than survival. He won't consider selling under any circumstances, which shows how much the land means beyond money. He still refuses to change his own methods, even as he prepares the next generation.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time and people should get ready, but not panic. Families and communities should look after their own. I'd say the same at the mart.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, I'd be past it by then, sitting by the fire with Rosa and an old dog. It'd be Daniel's world, not mine. That's sad, but it's how it's meant to go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd farm as I do and hand over to Daniel bit by bit, so he's running it by the time I'm sixty-five. I'd keep saving and pay off the hay shed. I wouldn't change how I farm, but I'd stop saying no to Daniel's ideas.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but at peace with it, mostly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Ten years takes you to sixty-eight. Does this one feel different?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell him it's his farm now, and I'd trust him. I might stand at the gate grumbling, mind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If Daniel wanted to bring robots onto the hill in ten years, what would you say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That the dogs stay. Even if the robots do the gathering, I want a dog on Blackstone till the day the farm's gone.

S4.say: He'd tell people at the market that ten years is long enough to get ready without panic, and families and communities should look after their own.
S4.think: Privately he expects to be retired by then, by the fire with his wife and an old dog, leaving it as his nephew's world, which is sad but right.
S4.do: Farms as he does and hands over to his nephew bit by bit so he's running it by sixty-five. Keeps saving, pays off the hay shed loan and stops blocking his nephew's ideas.
S4.feel: Uneasy but mostly at peace with it.
S4.quote: Even if the robots do the gathering, I want a dog on Blackstone till the day the farm's gone.
S4.fieldNote: With a decade, he accepts change as part of the natural order of generations. His resistance softens into trust in his nephew rather than any change in his own habits. The dogs stand for everything he values about the old way.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, without a doubt. What would help is someone stopping the big companies from buying up farmland with robot money, and fair prices for lamb. I don't want a cheque, I want a fair market.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Whether we'd still be farmers if a robot did the work. I don't think you would. A farmer's someone who answers for the land, and a machine doesn't answer to anyone.

headlineQuote: A farmer's someone who answers for the land, and a machine doesn't answer to anyone.
portrait: Rafael Young, 58, farms Blackstone, his grandfather's hill sheep and cattle farm, with his brother, nephew and a hired shepherd, gathering the hill with his dogs Bess and Moss. He's devout, self-reliant and dead set against AI tools, and he trusts family and church far more than government. He's calm if AI fizzles and uneasy about prices under steady change, but alarmed by AGI in two years, which he sees as the end of his family's way of life. With more time he focuses on passing the land safely to his nephew.
biggestWorry: AGI in two years worries him most, because it could collapse lamb prices and hand farmland to whoever owns the machines.
whatWouldHelp: Stopping big companies from buying farmland with robot money, and fair prices for lamb rather than government cheques.
